name: Grounds For Thought: August Lineup
description: Grounds for Thought: August 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesFour Thursday evenings. Four very different conversations. Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shops. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does.6th August: Shambhavi TiwariPossessed: The Ghost, The Asylum, The Priest, and the PeopleWhen someone in rural India is "possessed by a ghost," they encounter not just their family and their priest, but eventually — often — a psychiatrist. Two completely different frameworks for what has gone wrong, and what healing looks like. This session uses spirit possession across Indian cultural contexts to examine what happens when indigenous knowledge systems and clinical medicine cross paths. PhD researcher Shambhavi Tiwari, who has spent years in this space, asks: superstition, myth, knowledge system, or something else entirely?13th August: Dr. Vishwas ChitaleZoom In, Zoom Out: What India's Climate Risk Looks Like at Ground LevelEveryone has heard the national climate numbers. But zoom into a district, and the picture changes entirely — neighbouring areas with opposite risk profiles, and disaster plans built on averages too coarse to catch where the real danger sits. Dr. Vishwas Chitale, Fellow at CEEW, will walk us through India's climate risk from the national level down to your own neighbourhood — and then hand the tool to the room. Participants will pull up their own hometown's actual climate risk profile live, using CRAVIS, CEEW's climate intelligence platform. You'll leave having done a small piece of the research yourself.20th August: Antara ChakrabartyFrom Village to Viral: How Folk Music Got a Second LifeA seventeenth-century Sufi verse now has a hundred million YouTube views. The songs of Lalon Fakir, Bengal's wandering poet-saint, are uniting two Bengals and two centuries through a single melody. This session traces folk music's remarkable journey — from Punjab's Sufi shrines and Bengal's riverside Baul gatherings to studio stages and streaming platforms — and asks the questions nobody quite wants to answer. Who owns a folk song? What happens when heritage becomes entertainment? Does something get lost in translation, or does it simply learn a new way to survive? Expect live music, a few surprises, and a fresh way of listening to songs you may already love.27th August: Sunaina SaxenaWhat is a Clean Street Worth?Why are two seemingly identical houses priced so differently? This session explores one of environmental economics' most elegant tools, hedonic pricing, to answer a question most of us have never thought to ask: does the cleanliness of a neighbourhood have a measurable economic value? Through stories, discussion, and simple examples, researcher Sunaina Saxena explores how clean streets, reliable waste collection, and a healthy living environment become embedded in housing prices — and what that reveals about our cities and the choices we make about where we live.

name: The Making of a Serial Offender
description: Join us for an evening that begins with a simple question: what does a serial offender look like? The answer may be more unsettling than you think.About the LectureThe point is not that everyone is a criminal. The point is that none of us can recognise one by looking.This lecture explores how criminal profiling moved beyond outdated assumptions about "criminal faces" to become one of the most fascinating tools in modern investigations. Why do some individuals cross lines that most never do? What can behaviour tell us about risk, intent, and future offending? And how can India build more rigorous behavioural science frameworks for criminal investigation?Part psychology, part criminology, and part investigative science, this session offers a rare glimpse into the complex process of understanding criminal behaviour.About the SpeakerMr. Rithin Joseph is an Assistant Professor at the School of Behavioural Forensics, National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU), Delhi. name: The Limits of Computation
description: Join us for a lecture that traces one dangerous idea through three brilliant, broken minds:In 1891, Georg Cantor gave us set theory, and then spent years battling for his peace of mind. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved that any system of logic cannot capture all truths, and later descended into deep paranoia. In 1936, Alan Turing identified problems that no computer can ever solve; and met a tragic end.Three of history's most brilliant minds, circling the same dangerous idea.This lecture plays with diagonalisation — the beautifully unsettling proof technique at the heart of all three discoveries — and explores what it reveals about the limits of logic, mathematics and computation itself. They seem to press back on the people who find them.The session explores:What diagonalisation is, and why the same idea kept resurfacing across a century of mathematicsHow Cantor's set theory, Gödel's incompleteness theorems and Turing's halting problem are secretly the same argumentWhat it means for a system of logic to be unable to capture all truthsWhy some of history's most brilliant thinkers found this particular idea so disturbingAbout the SpeakerDr. Aalok Thakkar is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Ashoka University.
